ca_rock_garden_valley_left_side.blurb: A popular east-facing wall in the Lost Horse part of Joshua Tree National Park, at roughly 4,200 feet. Most of the twenty-five lines are single-pitch trad on cracks and faces, with a few top-rope problems, and the grades run mainly from 5.6 up to 5.10, topping out around 5.11. The granite is textured and protects well, and a row of anchors along the rim makes setting ropes quick. Because it faces east it catches the morning sun and drops into shade by afternoon, which suits warm days. It is busier than the quieter middle section of the valley, so expect company on good weekends. Bring a standard trad rack.

ca_main_wall_left.blurb: The left half of the Main Wall at the Pie Shop, on the south shore of Lake Tahoe near the airport at about 6,800 feet. It is a slab-and-corner formation, mostly trad with a handful of sport lines and one top-rope. The twenty-five routes start around 5.5 and reach 5.13 at the top end, though the bulk sit in the 5.7 to 5.10 band, making it a good fit for moderate leaders. The lower elevation and southern exposure of the Pie Shop make it climbable earlier in the year than higher Sierra crags, but it can get hot in midsummer. The stone is solid, and the setting is open with views over the basin.

ca_south_face_20.blurb: The south face is the main and most-climbed side of this small formation in the Quail Springs part of Joshua Tree National Park, just across the road from the picnic area. The twenty-five routes are mostly short trad cracks and corners with a few top-rope lines, mainly 5.7 to 5.10 with a couple of harder outings. The walk from the car is very short, so it makes an easy stop for a quick session or a warm-up near the road. Being south-facing it gets plenty of sun, so cooler days or early starts are the comfortable choice. A descent route leads off the back of the formation.

ca_6_gpa_right_side.blurb: The right-hand portion of Glacier Point Apron, a big granite slab at the east end of Yosemite Valley above the Happy Isles area. All twenty-five climbs are trad, ranging from short single pitches to longer multi-pitch slab lines, with grades from 5.7 through the 5.10s and 5.11s up to a few 5.12s and one 5.13. Climbing here is friction-dependent on smooth rock, with protection that blends bolts and natural gear, so it rewards good footwork and a calm head. The base is reached by a short trail from the valley floor, and the right side tends to be quieter than the classic central lines.

ca_faulty_tower.blurb: A shady, east-facing wall in the Central Gorge of the Owens River Gorge near Bishop, in the Eastern Sierra, a short stroll upriver from the Warm Up Wall. Nearly all of the twenty-five routes are bolted sport lines on volcanic tuff, with one or two needing a few pieces of gear. Grades span from 5.8 into the 5.14 range, but the heart of it is 5.11 and 5.12, so it suits stronger sport climbers. Some lines start from a ledge reached by easy fifth-class ground, and the upper left tier sees few visitors. The gorge can be hot in summer, and the shade here helps.

ca_castle_rock_proper.blurb: The central formation of Castle Rock State Park in the Santa Cruz Mountains above Silicon Valley, at about 3,200 feet. The sandstone is soft and friction-heavy, shaped into pockets, caves and ridges. Most of the twenty-five climbs are boulder problems from V1 to V5, plus a few short top-rope and trad lines from 5.5 to about 5.11. Landings are fairly forgiving, the forest is shady, and the style rewards smearing over pulling on holds. Fall through spring is the comfortable window, since summer can feel muggy, and the rock weakens when wet, so give it a day or two after rain. Weekends draw crowds.

ca_stained_glass_flyboy_area.blurb: A bouldering sector at the west end of the Buttermilks Main hillside near Bishop, in the Eastern Sierra at around 6,400 feet. The twenty-five problems cover a wide spread, from V0 up through the mid grades into the V9 to V11 range, so there is something for most levels. The boulders are big glacial blocs of coarse, grippy rock with patina edges and flat, sandy landings, though some tops are tall and the downclimbs need scouting. Bring plenty of pads and finger tape. Rattlesnakes show up in warm months, and heavy foot traffic is harming the desert plants, so stay on the established paths.
